# Restorative Agrisolar Design {.unnumbered}

::: {.draft-note}
**Working draft, circulated for comment.** Some citations are
[not yet verified](chapters/sources.qmd) and are marked where they appear, and the
[open issues](chapters/open-issues.qmd) record what this document has deliberately
not settled.
:::

::: {.welcome}
Solar and farming want the same flat, open, well-drained ground. An array can carry pollinator habitat or gravel, slow runoff or redirect it, shade stock, retire irrigation demand, or help sustain a farm. Those are design decisions.

[**Agrisolar**](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-agrisolar) names solar generation on agricultural land, whether or not production continues below it. [**Agrivoltaics**](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics) is the narrower case of crops or livestock inside the [footprint](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence). Direct crop production under or between panels is under two percent of built practice, and it carries a large share of the research attention [@stid2022; @macknick2022]. A working vocabulary has to describe the other ninety-eight percent as precisely as it describes the exception.

Where the boundary is drawn decides what counts. Most accounting stops at the fence line, the top of the modules, and a meter into the soil. This document draws it around the farm operation and the community hosting it, so a lease that keeps a farm solvent, the water leaving the field, and the habitat next door are all inside the frame.

[**Restorative agrisolar design**](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-restorative) holds that ecological, hydrological, and community function belong among a project's objectives. This document gives that claim a vocabulary that can be tested on real ground.
:::

## A shared language

A [solar grazier](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-rangevoltaics), township planner, hydrologist, and developer can describe the same eighty acres in incompatible terms. This lexicon is for the people deciding what an array does to an operation and a place.

Those decisions are being made now, and mostly in an information-poor setting: townships write ordinances without comparable data, developers and neighbors argue past each other, and several states have moved permitting authority away from the communities that host the projects [@susskind2022; @bessette2024]. Shared terms will not resolve those arguments. They let people find out what they are actually arguing about.

The build-out is not a forecast. Around 15,000 ground-mounted arrays already cover some 3,000 km² of the United States; roughly half of that ground was cropland beforehand and another third agricultural grassland [@stid2022; @sturchio2025croplands]. A net-zero grid by 2050 could put solar on 60,000–90,000 km², roughly 1% of the contiguous United States [@larson2021]. Most of what comes next will be farmland too.

## How the language works

A project is a long list of decisions, and almost all of them fall into six groups: how much ground to take, which ground, what gets built on it, what grows there and how the place is run, who holds the asset, and what the parties signed. Those are the [design levers](chapters/design-levers.qmd), and they are the spine of everything else here. The [pressures](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-design-pressures) push on them, and what comes out the far end is a project's scale, its position on the [sharing–sparing axis](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-sharing-sparing), and the [functions](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-restorative-function) the ground ends up performing.

![How the pieces fit. The levers are the only things anyone can actually change; everything to their left is a force acting on them, and everything to their right is a consequence of how they were set.](figures/fig_language_structure.svg){#fig-language-structure}

Two levers carry enough internal structure to need a chapter each. **Scale** becomes the [scale transect](chapters/scale-transect.qmd), five calibration points from the farmstead to the region, because interconnection, decision-making, and ground management all move together along it. **Siting, structure, and management** jointly produce a position on the [sharing–sparing axis](chapters/sharing-sparing-axis.qmd), which records what happened to agricultural production: whether farming continues inside the footprint is settled by what was built and what is grown, and what the ground was beforehand is settled by where the array went.

:::  {#sec-aim-not-dimensions}
**The aim is argued; the dimensions are left to the site.** This document takes a position on what agrisolar is *for*, and refuses to fix a clearance height or a row spacing, because the same lever settings that restore ground in one region deplete it in another. [Regionality](chapters/regionality.qmd) is where that gets explicit.
:::

## Where to start

::: {.routes}
**If you have land in mind and want to know what is possible on it**, go to
[what appears at each scale](chapters/archetypes.qmd#sec-by-zone), which sets out the forms that
recur at each size of project, from a barn roof to a regional complex, with what each one asks of the
ground.

**If you are weighing a specific proposal**, start with the
[design levers](chapters/design-levers.qmd) to see which decisions are still open, then the
[design pressures](chapters/design-pressures.qmd) for the forces pushing on each one and the
conflicts worth arguing about openly.

**If you want to know what is not yet known**, [open issues and research needs](chapters/open-issues.qmd) collect the measurements nobody has made, the figures that circulate without a source, and the counterexamples that would test
the claims here.

**If you are trying to pin down a term** someone has used, the
[alphabetical index](chapters/index-alphabetical.qmd) lists everything this document defines,
and the search box at the top of every page finds the rest.

:::

## Joining in

This is a working document, and it improves by being disagreed with. Corrections,
counterexamples, and proposed terms are welcome as issues or pull requests on
[GitHub](https://github.com/MSUHydrogeology/agrisolar_lexicon). Especially useful: an archetype
that recurs in your region and is missing here, a term that lands badly with the people who have
to use it, or a citation you can trace further than we have.
